title: Why My Students Spend the First Three Days Learning About Learning
author: SoL in the Wild
summary: A 7th grade World Studies teacher explains why they dedicate the first three days of the school year not to content but to explicitly teaching students how learning itself works. The rationale is that students spend thousands of hours in classrooms without ever being taught a mental model for memory and learning, despite being required to take notes, study, and complete projects that depend on understanding those processes. By front-loading metacognition, the teacher aims to help students understand not just what they'll do in class but why the classroom is structured the way it is and why particular instructional choices are made throughout the year. The piece positions this investment of instructional time as some of the most valuable learning students will do all year, reframing 'lost' content time as foundational cognitive-science groundwork.
points: Dedicates the first three days of the school year to teaching students how learning and memory work, before any content.
Argues most students go through school never given an explicit mental model for how learning actually happens.
Frames the investment as building buy-in: students understand why classroom routines and teaching choices are shaped the way they are.
Treats explaining the 'why' behind instructional design as a form of transparency that pays off across the year.
Reframes metacognition instruction as high-value use of instructional time, not a distraction from content.
quotes: For the first three days of school, my 7th grade World Studies students won't learn about the world.
we'll spend three days studying something just as important: how they learn and how I teach them based on how they learn
if students understand how learning works, they are far more likely to understand why our classroom works the way it does and why I teach them they way I do
Students spend thousands of hours in classrooms throughout their lives, yet very few, if any, are ever explicitly taught how memory and learning works.

They are required to take notes, answer questions, finish work at home, study for tests, and complete projects without ever being given a mental model for why those processes might, or in some cases, might not help them learn.
